narrative:
The model determined that you have a 99.2% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a very high bar for predicted success, this high risk of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by their importance. Your academic performance in law school played the biggest role. Both your first-year and third-year class rankings placed you in the second decile, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked around the sixth decile. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. 

Family income was the third most influential factor. Your upper-middle income background actually worked slightly in your favor compared with other applicants, but it was not nearly enough to offset the academic concerns.

Taken together, these elements made the model conclude that the likelihood of you passing the bar on the first try was extremely low. Gender and race played no part in this outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if possible, consider retaking key courses, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that place less weight on early law-school performance. Building a stronger overall profile before reapplying could meaningfully change future predictions. (218 words)
